hops.title: Say it: a dry bean is a camper waiting for an alarm
hops.text: Show your child a dry bean and say, "This bean is a camper in a sleeping bag, waiting for water to ring its alarm." Stay with your child, keep beans from children under 4 (choking risk), and skip tasting. At Michigan State University, some mullein seeds spent 141 years buried in sand, then sprouted after scientists dug them up.

sources.citation: Michigan State University, W. J. Beal Botanical Garden, "Beal Seed Experiment"
Fleming et al., "The 141-year period for Dr. Beal's seed viability experiment: A hybrid surprise," American Journal of Botany, 2023

hops.title: Compare it: a bean shoot leads with a bent elbow
hops.text: While standing still, have your child bend one arm and point their elbow up. Ask which part would poke through the dirt first if their arm were a bean shoot. A bean shoot does just that: its curved stem leads through gritty dirt, helping shield the soft baby leaves tucked behind it, then straightens in the light.

sources.citation: Biology LibreTexts, Ha, Morrow and Algiers, Botany, "4.6.4: Germination"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A green bean sprout coming out of dark soil with a curved, hooked stem sheltering tiny folded leaves.
image.caption: The bean shoot leads with its bend, which helps protect the tiny leaves as it pushes through soil.

hops.title: Point at it: acorns and squirrels under an oak
hops.text: On a walk, stand with your child under an oak and spot acorns on the ground. Point to them and leave them there: no tasting, and keep acorns out of reach of children under 4 (choking risk). Watch for gray squirrels too. They bury acorns and forget some, and those acorns can sprout into new oaks.

image.caption: Squirrels bury acorns and leave some behind to wake up as oak trees.

audio.title: Three playful ways to talk about waking seeds
audio.transcript:
Show your child a dry bean and see if it looks like a tiny pebble. Stay with them while the beans are out. Keep beans away from children under four, since they are a choking risk, and skip tasting the beans or the sprouts. A fun way to start is to say, "This bean is a camper in a sleeping bag, just waiting for water to ring its alarm." Back in eighteen seventy-nine, a botanist at Michigan State University buried twenty glass bottles of seeds in sand. Scientists now plan to dig up one bottle every twenty years. They dug up a bottle in twenty twenty-one, and some mullein seeds from it sprouted after spending one hundred forty-one years underground.

Look for the root first. Later, when you spot the curved shoot in your damp bag, try a little game. Stand next to your child and ask them to bend one arm and point their elbow up. Pretend their elbow is the first part of a bean shoot to poke through the dirt. A bean shoot really bends into a hook and leads with the bend, so the stem takes the rubbing from the gritty dirt, which helps protect the soft baby leaves tucked behind it. Once it reaches the light, it straightens up.

And on your next walk, stand with your child near an oak tree and look for acorns on the ground. Point to the acorns where they lie. Skip tasting, and keep acorns out of reach of children under four. Watch for gray squirrels too. Squirrels bury acorns and sometimes forget where they hid them, and those acorns can sprout into new oak trees. So the next time you see a squirrel digging, you can tell your child it might be planting a tree by accident.
